The Taimen (Hucho taimen) is widely regarded as the largest salmonid species in the world, with the most formidable individuals attaining an ultimate total length of 200 centimeters [Li = 200 centimeters], a remarkable measurement that firmly places this species among the apex freshwater predators of the Palearctic region. Despite its immense adult size, the species begins life as a remarkably small egg; the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a figure derived from the typical diameter of the ovum. This extraordinary disparity in mass between the tiny hatchling and the fully grown adult highlights an extreme ontogenetic trajectory that often spans multiple decades across the life cycle. Field surveys conducted across the Amur River basin have confirmed that a sexually mature female, capable of active reproduction, reaches a total length at puberty of approximately 50 centimeters [Lp = approximately 50 centimeters], though this developmental landmark is reached with considerable individual variation and is typically attained between four and six years of age.

Under the stable, cold-water thermal regime characteristic of the Siberian rivers this species inhabits, where the water temperature averages 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the maximum reproductive output of a female Taimen is substantial and well-documented. Specifically, a single gravid individual can produce approximately 121 eggs per day, which translates to an estimated total of 44,000 eggs produced across one spawning season [Ri = 44,000 eggs produced across one spawning season], with spawning occurring once annually [F_R_i = spawning occurring once annually]. This notably high fecundity represents an evolutionary adaptation to the extremely low survival rates experienced during the protracted yolk-sac larva phase that follows. The process of egg fertilisation is external and occurs over gravel beds during the spring spawning run. After the chorion ruptures and the alevin emerges, the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its internal yolk reserves before the critical onset of exogenous feeding, a period during which mortality is extremely high due to predation and environmental stressors.

The attainment of sexual maturation in Taimen is intimately tied to body size, and the corresponding somatic investment is substantial. Upon reaching puberty, a female Taimen has accumulated a wet weight of approximately 1,400 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,400 grams], a threshold that represents a considerable energetic investment in somatic growth before any resources are directed toward offspring production. This weight at puberty stands in stark contrast to the ultimate wet weight achieved by the largest adults, which can reach 92,300 grams [Wwi = 92,300 grams] in prime condition. Such a massive ultimate mass is a product of the species' long lifespan and its piscivorous feeding strategy, allowing it to dominate the food web. The weight gain from the fingerling stage to the reproductively viable organism involves a dramatic allometric shift, as the fish transitions from feeding on invertebrates to preying upon other fish species.

The maximum documented lifespan for the Taimen, recorded under the cool thermal conditions of its native habitat at 11 °C [T = 11 °C], approaches 55 years [am = 55 years]. This remarkable longevity is among the greatest recorded for any salmonid species. A fish of this age would have experienced numerous spawning seasons, demonstrating the iteroparous nature of the species, where individuals spawn multiple times across their lives. The slow rate of senescence in this species is linked to its cold-water physiology and the relatively low metabolic costs associated with tissue upkeep in such an environment. Field studies using otolith microchemistry have confirmed ages exceeding five decades in large specimens from undisturbed river systems, underscoring the critical importance of habitat preservation for maintaining stable populations. The death of such an aged individual is typically the result of natural mortality following a gradual post-reproductive decline.

Comparative life-history data across the genus Hucho reveal that the Taimen's life history strategy is characterised by exceptionally slow juvenile growth followed by a period of rapid mass gain leading up to first spawning. The species attains a maximum of 55 years [am = 55 years] at 11 °C [T = 11 °C], with the growth curve such that the length at puberty, approximately 50 centimeters [Lp = approximately 50 centimeters], is not attained for nearly half a decade. The estimated production of 44,000 eggs per season [Ri = 44,000 eggs per season] by a single large female, though impressive, represents a striking trade-off with egg size, as the small ova lead to a neonate wet weight at birth of just 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. This combination of traits—staggering longevity, delayed maturation, and high fecundity balanced by minute offspring—positions the Taimen as a classic K-selected strategist in the harsh, resource-limited environments of northern Asia.
